## Simple explanation

Text classification assigns labels to text. Examples include sorting
support tickets by topic, detecting spam, or identifying the language of a
message.

## Technical explanation

A text classifier maps a text representation to one or more labels. It may
use bag-of-words features with a linear model, a pretrained encoder, or a
generative model. Tasks can be binary, multiclass, or multilabel, and
evaluation should match the label structure and class distribution.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Classification supports routing, moderation, analytics, and information
extraction workflows. Production systems need reliable labels, threshold
selection, drift monitoring, and clear handling of ambiguous or
out-of-scope text.

## How it works

Text is normalized or tokenized and mapped to features or contextual
representations. A model predicts class scores, which are converted into
labels using an argmax or per-label thresholds. Performance is measured
against labeled held-out examples.

## Practical example

A ticket-routing system can classify incoming messages into product
areas. Evaluate precision and recall for each category, especially rare
categories, and provide a fallback when confidence is insufficient.

## Common misconceptions

- A classifier's top label is not necessarily reliable, especially for
  inputs unlike its training data.
- Accuracy can hide poor performance on rare classes.
